counterevidence.claim: Cook et al 2013's ~97% is a robust, method-independent measure that settles the general 'scientists agree' claim.
counterevidence.evidence: Tol 2016 argues Cook et al 2013 finds different results than previous studies and omits tests for systematic differences between raters.
counterevidence.qualification: An independent published comment (different author) contesting method; the Cook et al 2016 synthesis responds that estimates still converge at 90-100% among publishing scientists and near 97% among experts.

dependencies.description: The aggregated public claim depends on the NASA consensus statement, which itself cites multiple studies.
Reproducing Cook 2013's 97.1% depends on the Table 3 endorse count and the position breakdown.
Cook 2013 also reports an author self-rating phase (97.2%), a distinct method within the same study.
Doran 2009's 97.4% depends on the specialist subsample's question-2 yes-rate (75 of 77).
Comparing the estimates depends on the Cook 2016 synthesis, whose 90-100% range spans distinct populations.
A further distinct lineage (Anderegg et al 2010, 97-98% of the 200 most-published) is reported via the Cook 2016 synthesis.
The represented disagreement depends on Tol 2016's published comment on Cook 2013.

license.source_material: Cook 2013, Cook 2016, and Tol 2016 are CC-BY-3.0; NASA content is US-Government work but marked unassessed pending line-item check; Doran & Zimmerman 2009 is under AGU copyright and quoted minimally.

limitations: The Tol 2014 Energy Policy re-analysis (doi:10.1016/j.enpol.2014.04.045) was not independently retrieved (subscription-gated); the Tol-Cook disagreement is represented via the open-access ERL 2016 exchange instead.
The NASA carrier and Doran 2009 licenses are marked unassessed; their quotes are held under the tighter unknown-license length limit.
Cook 2013 and Cook 2016 share lead author John Cook, so they are not independent lineages and are not counted as such.

question: When public statements report that about 97% of scientists agree humans cause climate change, which distinct studies does that figure aggregate, and do Cook et al 2013 abstract ratings, Doran and Zimmerman 2009's survey of scientists, and the Cook et al 2016 synthesis measure the same population and quantity?

claim_atoms.text: Public 'about 97% of scientists agree' statements such as NASA's aggregate several methodologically distinct studies rather than one measurement: Cook et al 2013's 97.1% is the endorsement rate among abstracts expressing a position on AGW; Doran and Zimmerman 2009's 97.4% is the yes-rate among 77 surveyed specialist climatologists; and the Cook et al 2016 synthesis reports a 90%-100% range across populations, which Tol 2016 disputes. The estimates converge near 97% but measure different populations and quantities.
Cook 2013: 97.1% among abstracts expressing a position (3896 endorsing)
Doran 2009: 97.4% of surveyed specialist climatologists (75 of 77)
Cook 2016 synthesis: 90%-100% of publishing climate scientists
NASA aggregates multiple studies into an 'about 97%' consensus message
Doran & Zimmerman 2009 survey of specialist climatologists
Cook 2013 rated 11 944 abstracts; Doran 2009 surveyed 79 specialist climatologists
credential-free HTTPS retrieval of archived version-of-record captures for all five sources
Cook 2013 sampled abstracts published from 1991 to 2011
abstract-position ratings, a scientist survey, and society statements measure distinct populations, not one

results.interpretation: The public '97% of scientists' message is broadly supported by convergent evidence, but it is an aggregate over distinct populations (rated abstracts, surveyed specialists, publication analyses) rather than a single measured fraction of all scientists, and it is often mis-attributed specifically to Cook 2013.
results.proposition: Public 'about 97% of scientists agree' statements such as NASA's aggregate several methodologically distinct studies rather than one measurement: Cook et al 2013's 97.1% is the endorsement rate among abstracts expressing a position on AGW; Doran and Zimmerman 2009's 97.4% is the yes-rate among 77 surveyed specialist climatologists; and the Cook et al 2016 synthesis reports a 90%-100% range across populations, which Tol 2016 disputes. The estimates converge near 97% but measure different populations and quantities.

results.warrant: NASA states the aggregate and cites the studies; Cook 2013, Doran 2009, and Cook 2016 report their own figures and populations; Tol 2016 supplies the published disagreement; the two reproduced calculations recover 97.1% and 97.4%.

scope.comparison_target: The public 'about 97% of scientists agree' message versus the distinct populations and methods of the studies it aggregates.
scope.excluded: The truth of anthropogenic warming itself, sources not retrieved (e.g. the Tol 2014 Energy Policy re-analysis), and public statements other than the NASA carrier.
scope.included: Five public primary sources - the NASA consensus carrier, Cook et al 2013, Doran & Zimmerman 2009, Cook et al 2016, and Tol 2016 - and the exact figures and populations they report.

search_notes: Prior-art check: distinct from the accepted dossiers and from the needs-evidence receipt PR #76 (a single-source Cook-2013-only audit); this successor adds the carrier plus the survey, synthesis, and critique lineages requested in the PR #76 review.
